S02.text: Students already enrolled and borrowing before July twenty twenty-six keep Grad PLUS for up to three more academic years, or for the time left in their program if that is shorter. New students like Leah still have the basic federal loan, a Direct Unsubsidized loan, up to twenty thousand five hundred dollars a year and one hundred thousand dollars total, with higher limits in professional programs like medicine or law. When a program costs more than that after other aid, the rest can come from a private lender, and that's where Leah's two offers come from. Same lender, same amount, two kinds of rate.

When a program costs more than that after other aid, the rest can come from a private lender, and that's where Leah's two offers come from. Same lender, same amount, two kinds of rate.

S03.text: Both are for fifty thousand dollars over ten years, illustrative numbers, not a real lender's offer. The variable loan's first payment is five hundred ninety-three dollars and fifty-one cents, about forty dollars less a month than the fixed six hundred thirty-three dollars and thirty-eight cents. A fixed rate never changes, so neither does the payment. A variable rate follows a market interest rate, so the rate and the payment rise and fall with it, and nobody knows where it goes next. The head start is the fixed rate minus the variable rate's starting rate; it is negative when the variable rate starts higher. Leah's fixed rate is nine percent and her variable rate starts at seven point five percent, so her head start is one point five points. A point here means one percentage point of interest. Real offers differ, so a head start can be bigger, smaller, zero, or negative.

S04.text: This video replays Leah's illustrative loan through every ten-year stretch of U.S. interest rates since January nineteen fifty-four. Each replay moves her rate up and down exactly as much as the three-month Treasury bill rate moved in that stretch of history, and the data is U.S. only. "Worth it" gets one plain meaning here: how often the variable loan cost more in total interest than the nine percent fixed loan, and how much more at worst. Then the replay moves the head start, from three points down to minus one point, to see where that history changes. By the end there's a line that any real offer can be held up against, including yours. This is history, not a forecast.

S05.text: [curious] And the first result looks like a contradiction. Leah's variable rate rose above nine percent at some point in seventy-six point two percent of stretches, about three in four. Yet it cost more in total interest in fourteen point two percent, about one in seven. That one in seven is made of two very different parts: twenty-eight point four percent, more than one in four, for starts from nineteen fifty-four to nineteen eighty, and three point five percent, about one in thirty, from nineteen eighty-one on; the worst stretch, from April nineteen seventy-seven, cost eleven thousand two hundred nineteen dollars more. The reason both are true is the head start.

S06.text: Every month the variable rate sits below nine percent, Leah pays less interest than on the fixed loan, and that saving builds a cushion. The cushion grows fastest at the start, when she owes the most, so every point of rate is charged on the biggest balance. When the rate later climbs above nine percent, the extra interest has to use up that cushion before the variable loan has cost more overall. A short jump above nine percent only dents it; emptying it needs rates that rise early and stay high for years. In a stretch where rates drift down, the cushion just keeps growing.

S07.text: And the two halves of the record are very different. From nineteen fifty-four to nineteen eighty, the Treasury bill rate mostly climbed, in waves. It peaked at sixteen point three percent in May nineteen eighty-one, then mostly drifted down over the following decades, with big swings. Same loan, same head start; the only difference is where in history it began. Loans started in the climbing years often met rates that rose early and stayed high, and loans started after the peak mostly rode rates down. The best stretch began in August nineteen eighty-one, near that peak, and cost fifteen thousand two hundred ninety-five dollars less than the fixed loan. It belongs to the falling half, while the worst, April nineteen seventy-seven, belongs to the climbing half, where far more of Leah's stretches cost more.

S08.text: [serious] Here is Leah's same loan, started in April nineteen seventy-seven. It begins at seven point five percent, like every replay, and for a while her cushion grows. Then the Treasury bill rate climbs year after year, and her rate follows it, to nineteen point three percent at its highest. The cushion from her first months is soon gone, and every further month above nine percent adds to what she owes in interest. Her payment reaches eight hundred sixty-three dollars and thirty-six cents a month, against the fixed six hundred thirty-three dollars and thirty-eight cents. Over ten years, the fixed loan charges twenty-six thousand five dollars in interest. Leah's variable loan charges forty-three percent more interest than the fixed loan, the worst stretch in the whole replay. This replay has no rate cap; a real loan's cap, if low enough, would have made this worst case smaller.

S09.text: So far, every result has been for one pair of rates, seven point five percent against nine percent. So the replay ran again, holding the fixed rate at nine percent and moving only where the variable rate starts. Each starting point is a different offer someone could be holding. Leah's one point five points gives the split already heard, with her April nineteen seventy-seven worst. At two points, none of the starts from nineteen eighty-one on cost more, but twenty point four percent of the nineteen fifty-four-to-nineteen eighty starts still did, the worst by nine thousand four hundred seventy-two dollars. [thoughtful] At three points, still none from nineteen eighty-one on, but ten point five percent of the nineteen fifty-four-to-nineteen eighty starts cost more, the worst by six thousand thirty-three dollars.

S10.text: With a smaller head start, or a variable rate that starts higher, more stretches cost more in both halves, and the worst gets bigger. At every head start tested, the worst stretch began in April nineteen seventy-seven. And at every head start tested, some of the nineteen fifty-four-to-nineteen eighty starts still cost more. So, back to the question: how much lower does a variable rate have to start before the risk has been worth it? Measured as how often it cost more in total interest than the nine percent fixed loan, and how much more at worst, history gives two answers. From nineteen eighty-one on, a two point head start was enough every time; from nineteen fifty-four to nineteen eighty, even three points was not, and the worst still cost six thousand thirty-three dollars more. Which kind of history comes next is something no replay can show.

S12.text: [warm] Leah's illustrative offer sits at one point five points, short of that two-point mark, where stretches from both halves of history still cost more and the worst was eleven thousand two hundred nineteen dollars. A real offer has its own two rates, its own head start and its own place on the line. It also has what this replay leaves out: the lender's real index, a rate cap, a grace period, fees, and the borrower's own budget. The line doesn't say which offer is better; it shows what each head start meant in each kind of history. [calm] History, not a forecast.
